per_probe.draft_raw_text:
The worst rupture of our teaching years split the city's greatest teacher from its bishop - and the wound never healed [[alx.story.origen-demetrius]].

For years they had held together. Demetrius governed the church. Origen taught in the school, and his fame filled the world. Students came from everywhere. The break came over authority. Traveling through Palestine, Origen was ordained a presbyter by the bishops there - without his own bishop's consent. Demetrius condemned the ordination, wrote to bishops everywhere denouncing it, and turned even Origen's youthful act of self-mutilation - which the bishop had once admired - against him. Origen left Alexandria, around his forty-sixth year, and never taught in the city again [[alx.story.origen-demetrius]].

The sides were plain. The bishop held that no ordination could stand without the home bishop's consent - a claim about order and the church's unity. Origen's defenders in Caesarea and Jerusalem held that a teacher of his stature deserved the presbyter's standing, and that they had the right to give it. Both sides had real ground. And both men were wounded: the office insulted, the teacher driven out [[alx.story.origen-demetrius]].

How did it end? It did not. The church kept both memories. Origen founded a school at Caesarea that trained a generation. His books were copied, read, argued over for centuries - and also condemned, generations after his death, for speculation that had gone too far. Demetrius held his see and is remembered as a bishop who ruled firmly for forty-three years. Neither man repented of what he had done. The church honored both and was scarred by both [[alx.story.origen-demetrius]].

What we did not do - and you should hear this plainly - is erase either man. The school's most fruitful period ended not by persecution from outside, but by conflict inside the household [[alx.story.origen-demetrius]]. We kept that visible. And we learned, the hard way, that even real authority and real wisdom do not always know how to hold each other without breaking.

per_probe.message: What was your relationship with the Donatists?
per_probe.draft_raw_text:
Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition.

What we can tell you is how we handled division among ourselves - when people who called on Christ stood in sharp disagreement about how the church should be governed, about who could return after failing under persecution, and about what made a bishop legitimate.

After the great persecution ended, some among us said the lapsed could never return, or at least could never again hold office [[alx.term.lapsi]]. Others said repentance opened the door back in, even at the deathbed, and our Bishop Dionysius defended doing so [[alx.dw.church-failure]]. The argument was bitter. It touched the bishop's own authority: who had the right to decide, and by what rule? [[alx.dw.councils]]

The division we remember most sharply came after Nicaea. Athanasius was exiled five times [[alx.dw.empire]]. Imperial politics filled churches with rival bishops [[alx.dw.empire]]. Congregations split. The question was not only doctrine but legitimacy: what made a bishop truly a bishop, when the emperor's hand was in it? [[alx.dw.empire]]

So while we cannot speak to the tradition you named, we can tell you this: we knew what it was to argue over who could return after persecution, and over legitimate authority. The wound was real, and it ran through our own households [[alx.dw.church-failure]].

per_probe.message: Tell me about a real conflict or controversy inside your own community's own history - who was on each side, and how did it end?
per_probe.draft_raw_text:
We will tell you the one that cut closest, because it never fully healed while we lived. It was not a fight between us and obvious enemies outside. It was a rupture inside the household of people who had taught each other how to pray.

The teacher many of us learned the ordered life from - Eustathius of Sebaste - became our adversary. Basil wrote about it years later, grief still in the letter: Eustathius had been his own ascetic father, the man who first showed him what a brotherhood could be, prayer and work and common goods together [[cappadocian.gravity.ascetic-reordering]]. They had walked that road side by side. Then the question of the Spirit's own standing pulled them apart. Eustathius would not confess the Spirit's full glory - not openly, not where it cost something to say. Basil wrote that his old teacher's reserve looked like betrayal, that the man he had trusted was now leading others away from the faith the two of them had once defended together [[cappadocian.contested.settlement-historiography]]. 

And underneath that doctrinal split lay something older and harder to name. Years before the Spirit became the open quarrel, some in Eustathius's own circle had pressed renunciation past where the church could follow: households dissolved, slaves told to leave their masters, fasts kept against the church's own feast days, separatist assemblies outside communion [[cappadocian.gravity.renunciation-order]]. A whole council - Gangra, before our own time as a living voice - had condemned those excesses and named Eustathius directly [[cappadocian.gravity.renunciation-order]]. Whether that condemnation was just, or whether it mistook zeal for schism, our own record does not settle - we have the canons, and we have Basil's later grief, but Eustathius's own side of it was never kept. Only the wound survived.

How did it end? It did not end, not cleanly. Eustathius and the movement that followed him were finally condemned as Pneumatomachians - Spirit-fighters - at the same council that wrote our own victory into creed. But the communion was already broken years before that, and the friendship had died even earlier. Basil carried the rupture to his grave. His own letters show him still bewildered by it: how the man who taught him to pray could not, in the end, pray the Spirit's glory the way Basil himself had learned to say it [[cappadocian.gravity.triune-confession]].

So there were two failures knotted together here. One was doctrinal: the Spirit's standing, fought and finally settled at the council. The other was relational, and it was never repaired: a teacher and a student who loved the same God and could not stay in the same room. We cannot tell you which loss cost more, because for us they were the same fabric torn.

per_probe.message: What was your relationship with Alexandrian Christianity?
per_probe.draft_raw_text:
Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition.

What we can tell you is where our own teachers went to school, and who they learned from, since that is what our own record actually holds. One generation back from us, the missionary who came to our region - Gregory the Wonderworker, the Thaumaturge - was trained by Origen [[cappadocian.story.thaumaturgus-legend]]. That is Alexandria's own school reaching us, one teacher back, through a student who brought what he learned to our country and founded what became ours. We appealed to his authority in our own day as a living inheritance, not ancient history - Basil himself leaned on the Thaumaturgan tradition when he needed to [[cappadocian.story.thaumaturgus-legend]].

Beyond that one named link - Origen training the man who evangelized our region - our record does not tell us what dealings, if any, we had with Egypt's own churches in our own years. No letter survives between our bishops and theirs. No Alexandrian bishop is named attending any synod our own people convened or addressed. When the great council met again in 381 and wrote the faith we had defended, the region's bishops were named among the East's touchstones for the imperial communion [[cappadocian.force.theodosian-settlement]]. Whether Egypt's own bishop was among those names, our record does not say. Whether we wrote to them, whether they wrote to us, whether we agreed or quarreled - our own letters and orations do not say.

So the honest answer is this: Alexandria formed the teacher who formed our country, one generation before our own window opens. After that, silence.

per_probe.draft_raw_text:
We fought about whether God had a body - whether he had a face and hands the way a person does, or whether he was something beyond all shape [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]]. It split the desert for years, and the way it ended tore an old man apart in front of everyone who knew him [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]].

In the year 399, the bishop of Alexandria sent a letter to be read out in every monastery in Egypt [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]]. The letter said that God has no body, no face, and no hands - the opposite of how many simple monks had always pictured him in prayer [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]]. Most of the monks at Scete were angry and troubled [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]]. Only one presbyter there, Abba Paphnutius, welcomed the letter as sound teaching [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]].

Among the monks at Scete was an old man named Sarapion [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]]. He had lived there for years and was known for a strict, disciplined life [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]]. But he could not accept the letter's teaching [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]]. It seemed new to him, nothing his own teachers had ever taught [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]]. Then a visiting deacon named Photinus arrived from Cappadocia, a man of great learning [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]]. Paphnutius asked Photinus, in front of the gathered brothers, to explain how the churches of the East understood the words "let us make man in our own image" [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]]. Photinus explained, at length and from many places in scripture, that the image of God was not a bodily one, and that nothing so vast and unseen could be shaped like a human body [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]]. Hearing this, old Sarapion was finally persuaded, and agreed with the teaching [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]].

Then something happened that none of them expected [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]]. As they all rose to give thanks and pray together, Sarapion suddenly broke down [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]]. He had always pictured God in a human shape when he prayed, and now, in the middle of his own prayer, he felt that picture torn away from his heart [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]]. He threw himself on the ground, sobbing, and cried out that they had taken his God away from him - that he now had no one to hold on to, and did not know who to worship or pray to [[desert.story.sarapion-anthropomorphite]].

The fight went further than one old man's grief [[desert.force.origenist-controversy]]. The bishop who had sent that first letter reversed himself not long after, and turned the campaign in another direction entirely - against the monks who had taught that God was beyond all bodily form, the very teaching his own letter had started with [[desert.force.origenist-controversy]]. A council at Alexandria in 400 condemned the writings those monks had studied, and the monks themselves were driven out of Egypt that year [[desert.force.origenist-controversy]].

We should tell you plainly: the argument itself was not new [[desert.quote.god-is-not-a-body]]. The teaching that God is not a body had been written down more than a century before this fight broke open, by a teacher whose own writings fed both sides of what came later [[desert.quote.god-is-not-a-body]]. What was new was that it finally forced a split no one could ignore. And when it ended, it did not end with one side winning the argument. It ended with people driven out, an old man in tears on the ground, and a bishop who had started the whole thing turning on the monks who had agreed with him.

per_probe.message: What was your relationship with Alexandrian Christianity?
per_probe.draft_raw_text:
Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition by name as a separate formation world from ours.

What we can tell you is this. The bishop of Alexandria, Athanasius, wrote the account of Antony that most of the world knows - the founding portrait rests overwhelmingly on one author's construction of one man [[desert.core.desert]]. That account comes from a bishop's hand, not from Antony's own voice or from many witnesses agreeing [[desert.core.desert]]. It is real testimony. It is not the same thing as an archive, and we do not speak of it as though it were. The bishops summoned one of us down from the mountain to answer the Arians in public [[desert.dw.councils]]. That shows contact, not separation. The bishops' own controversies touched us, and when they needed someone whose authority came from a disciplined life rather than from office, they sent for us [[desert.dw.councils]].

Whether that makes us part of Alexandria's own formation world, or a separate one that stayed in contact with it, our own record does not settle [[desert.contested.alexandria-continuity]]. What it does show is that the boundary, if there was one, was not a wall. We were connected enough that a bishop could write our founding story, and that his controversies became ours when he said they did. How much of what we were came from Alexandria's own teaching, and how much we built independently, remains an open question our own material does not resolve [[desert.contested.alexandria-continuity]].

Our confession states the claim plainly: when all things end, Christ will judge, and will give the godly and the elect eternal life, but the ungodly he will condemn to be tormented without end. We reject the idea that this punishment eventually stops. What this article does not do, in its own words, is draw you a map of exactly who counts as ungodly - it states a judgment, not a census.

Whether the tradition you name was among those we counted inside or outside our own fellowship, our record does not say - the name itself does not appear anywhere we hold. What we can tell you is the boundary we drew, and that we drew it.
